items.label: Research question (aim)
items.prompt: Find the sentence in the INTRODUCTION that states the aims of the study.
items.model: (1) How common are smartphone addiction symptoms, and (2) do depression or anxiety independently predict smartphone addiction in Lebanese students?
items.why: Real articles often state aims ('This study aims to…') instead of a research question. This one has TWO aims.

items.label: Hypothesis
items.prompt: Does this article state a formal hypothesis (a prediction)?
options: Yes, but only in the Discussion
items.model: No. The Introduction ends with aims, not a prediction.
items.why: Not every published article states a hypothesis. Don't force an aim into a hypothesis.

items.label: Predictor and outcome
items.prompt: What are the main predictor variables and the outcome variable?
items.model: Predictors: depression and anxiety. Outcome: smartphone addiction level (total SPAI score).
items.why: In the analysis, depression/anxiety are the main independent variables and the SPAI score is the dependent variable (see the Methods on the regression models).

items.label: Conceptual definition
items.prompt: Find the sentence that gives a conceptual definition of a SMARTPHONE.
items.model: A mobile phone that performs many functions of a computer (touch screen, internet access, operating system for apps).
items.why: A quoted dictionary-style definition at the start of the Introduction tells you what the concept means.

items.label: Operational definition (smartphone addiction)
items.prompt: How was SMARTPHONE ADDICTION measured? Find the sentence that names the scale.
items.model: The 26-item Smartphone Addiction Inventory (SPAI), rated on a 4-point scale (total 26–104).
items.why: The scale is named in one sentence and described in the next few; any of them is accepted.

items.label: Operational definition (excessive use)
items.prompt: How did the authors define EXCESSIVE smartphone use?
items.model: At least 5 hours of smartphone use on a weekday (the median).
items.why: This is an operational definition: it turns 'excessive use' into a measurable cut-off.

items.label: Operational definition (depression)
items.prompt: How were DEPRESSION and ANXIETY measured?
items.model: Brief screeners PHQ-2 (depression) and GAD-2 (anxiety); a score of 3 or more counted as screening positive.
items.why: The screeners are named in one sentence and explained in the following ones.

items.label: General method
items.prompt: What general method did this study use?
items.model: Cross-sectional survey: one questionnaire at one point in time, no manipulation.
items.why: The authors call it cross-sectional in the title and limitations; nothing was manipulated.

items.label: Sample
items.prompt: Find the sentence in the METHODS that describes who the participants were and where they came from.
items.model: 688 undergraduates at Notre Dame University, Lebanon, recruited from general education science courses.
items.why: Sample details appear in the Abstract, Methods and Results; the Methods sentence is the best answer.

items.label: Sampling method
items.prompt: What sampling method did the researchers use to select students?
items.model: Simple random sampling, followed by an email invitation.
items.why: Look for how students were 'selected' in the Methods.

items.label: Research gap
items.prompt: Find the sentence that shows the research gap. (The word 'gap' is never used.)
items.model: Earlier studies didn't control for many confounding variables at the same time when testing depression and anxiety as predictors.
items.why: '…they fell short of controlling…' signals a weakness in earlier research, which is the gap this study fills.

items.label: Control variables
items.prompt: Find the sentence listing the variables controlled for in the FINAL (fully adjusted) model.
items.model: Age, personality type, class, age at first smartphone use, weekday use and reasons for use.
items.why: Controlled variables (confounders) are adjusted for so the effect of depression/anxiety can be seen on its own.

items.label: Key finding
items.prompt: After controlling for confounders, were depression and anxiety significant predictors of smartphone addiction?
items.model: Both: depression β = 0.201, p < .001; anxiety β = 0.122, p = .034.
items.why: Check the final model in the Results: both p values are below .05.

items.label: Strongest predictor
items.prompt: Which variable was the STRONGEST predictor of smartphone addiction?
items.model: Excessive smartphone use (5+ hours on a weekday), β = 0.26.
items.why: Compare the beta values: the largest β shows the strongest predictor. It wasn't depression or anxiety.

items.label: Authors' explanation
items.prompt: No named theory is used. Find the sentence in the CONCLUSION where the authors propose an explanation for the findings.
items.model: Type A students with high stress and low mood may lack coping and mood-management skills, making them prone to smartphone addiction.
items.why: When there's no formal theoretical framework, authors often offer a tentative explanation using hedges like 'it could be' or 'we posit'.

items.label: Study strength
items.prompt: Find the sentence where the authors describe a STRENGTH of their study.
items.model: They controlled for many confounders at the same time, and used validated tools.
items.why: Strengths and limitations are often in the same subsection; strengths come first here.

items.label: Limitation (design)
items.prompt: Find the limitation about the study DESIGN.
items.model: Cross-sectional design, so relationships can't be interpreted as causal.
items.why: A cross-sectional design measures everything at once, so it can't show cause and effect.

items.label: Limitation (data)
items.prompt: Find the limitation about how the DATA were collected.
items.model: Self-reported data may be inaccurate (not wanting to reveal vulnerabilities; recall bias).
items.why: Self-report is a common limitation; the authors name two reasons it may be inaccurate.

items.label: Causal language
items.prompt: Which sentence best reports the main finding?
options: Depression was associated with higher smartphone addiction
items.ans: Depression was associated with higher smartphone addiction
items.model: 'Associated with', because the design is cross-sectional.
items.why: Even though the authors call depression a 'predictor', a cross-sectional design can't establish cause.
